What are they? Comfortable wireless over-ear headphones with excellent sound, improved noise cancellation, and long battery life.

Who are they best for? Travelers and frequent listeners seeking great sound and longer battery life for less than AirPods Max.

Who should skip them? Bargain hunters who can save with the Momentum 4, or buyers prioritizing the strongest noise cancellation.

The Momentum 4 was already one of our favourite over-ear headphones, and the new Momentum 5 provides a number of improvements that help to improve both sound quality and noise-cancellation. This update is a little more expensive though, now costing $399.95/£329.99, although the Momentum 4 is still widely available online with a reduced price of around $299.00/£199.00 so that’s still a good option if you’re looking for a bargain.

Available in a variety of colours, the Momentum 5 looks very similar to its predecessor, with large earpieces that house 42mm drivers and are thickly padded for comfort. Despite the large earpieces, the headphone only weighs 290g – compared to 386g for Apple’s AirPods Max – so they’re light and comfortable enough to wear for long periods of time, and Sennheiser also includes a sturdy travelling case to protect the headphones when you’re out and about. Battery life is impressive too, lasting for around 57 hours even when using noise-cancellation – compared to just 20 hours for the AirPods Max – which makes the Momentum 5 a great option for long journeys. And, if the battery does run down then you can switch to wired mode, with both USB-C and 3.5mm cables included (although the 3.5mm cable has a 2.5mm jack for connecting to the headphones, which could cause problems if you lose the cable and need to buy a replacement).

Bluetooth support has been updated for this model, stepping up to Bluetooth 5.4 and aptX Lossless/Adaptive, along with AAC for Apple devices, and support for Dolby Atmos spatial audio. The Momentum 5 is also certified for hi-res audio, and provides an impressive frequency response of 6Hz – 40KHz when using Bluetooth or a USB-C connection, which results in excellent sound quality.

It digs really deep for the rumbling electronic bass effects on Max Richter’s Shadow Journal, while the spatial audio creates an atmospheric soundstage for the track’s hazy, ambient sounds. There’s clarity on the higher frequencies too, with the violins cutting through haze to add a sense of urgency to the piece. Switching to something heavier and harder, the Momentum 5 does a great job of balancing the sonic mash-up of Sing Along by Sturgill Simpson. The fuzzy guitar riffs have a head-banging power that drives the track forward, while the precise, ticking percussion is irresistibly catchy. The synths wail with dance-floor energy, and the bass drop toward the end has a real kick to it.

The noise-cancellation has been improved as well. The Momentum 5 can now match the AirPods Max when it comes to blocking out low-frequency sounds such as the rumble of an aircraft engine. It does a good job with higher frequency sounds too, although the AirPods Max still has an edge in that area. Mind you, the AirPods Max are around $200/£200 more expensive so the Momentum 5 is really good value for money, especially with that outstanding battery life for long journeys.

Should you buy the Sennheiser Momentum 5 Wireless?

The Momentum 5 Wireless is a strong choice if you want excellent sound, effective noise cancellation, and enough battery life for long journeys. Its deep, firm bass brings energy to electronic music and rock, while clear higher frequencies keep instruments distinct. The lightweight design and generous padding also make it comfortable for extended listening.

For Apple users, AAC support, Dolby Atmos spatial audio, and USB-C audio provide useful flexibility. Noise cancellation matches the AirPods Max for low-frequency rumble, although Apple’s headphones retain an advantage with higher-frequency sounds. The Momentum 5 counters with a considerably lower price and around 57 hours of battery life with noise cancellation enabled.

At $399.95/£329.99, it offers a compelling balance of sound, comfort, and endurance. However, bargain hunters should consider the Momentum 4, available for around $299/£199. The improved sound and noise cancellation make the newer model appealing, but the older headphones remain a good budget option.

Buying advice: What to look for when buying headphones

Below, we run through what to look for when choosing over-ear headphones for your iPhone or Mac, from sound quality and comfort to Apple features, lossless audio, noise cancellation and battery life.

Which headphone features matter for iPhone and Mac users?

Sound quality, comfort and reliable connectivity should come first. AAC support is useful for Bluetooth listening on Apple devices, but it isn’t required for basic compatibility. Check which additional features work with your iPhone, iPad and Mac, including easy pairing, automatic switching, hands-free Siri and Find My. These vary between models – even within Apple’s AirPods and Beats ranges.

Bluetooth multipoint lets compatible headphones maintain connections to two devices, making it useful for moving between an iPhone and Mac. Check how switching works in practice, rather than assuming it behaves like Apple’s automatic switching. Also check whether the manufacturer’s iPhone app offers equalizer controls and firmware updates.

Prioritize listening assessments over driver size or frequency-response claims. Look for clear vocals, audible detail and bass that suits your taste without overwhelming the music.

Can I listen to Apple Music lossless through headphones?

Yes, but the connection matters. Standard Bluetooth playback from an iPhone or Mac uses compression, even when you select a lossless track in Apple Music. A compatible wired connection is the straightforward way to hear lossless audio.

AirPods Max 2 and the first-generation USB-C AirPods Max support lossless playback over USB-C with current software and firmware. Some competing wireless headphones, including Beats Studio Pro, also offer USB audio. However, a USB-C charging port doesn’t necessarily support audio, so check before buying.

Traditional headphones with a 3.5mm plug are another option. Depending on your device, you may need an adapter or an external digital-to-analog converter (DAC). The supported resolution depends on the entire connection; wired listening doesn’t automatically guarantee support for Apple Music’s highest-resolution recordings. See our guide to DACs and lossless audio on iPhone and Mac.

Some headphones include a wireless transmitter. Check its compatibility and supported formats: adding a transmitter doesn’t automatically make playback lossless.

How much noise cancellation do I need?

For frequent flights, train journeys or noisy workplaces, prioritize effective active noise cancellation (ANC). It is particularly useful against steady sounds such as engine drone. Performance against conversations and sudden noises varies, so look for listening-test results rather than relying on manufacturers’ claims.

Passive isolation comes from the earcups sealing around your ears. A good fit helps both isolation and sound quality. Transparency or ambient modes use microphones to let you hear your surroundings without removing the headphones – useful when listening for announcements or maintaining awareness while walking.

If you make frequent calls, assess microphone performance separately: effective listening ANC doesn’t guarantee clear speech for the person you’re calling.

What makes over-ear headphones comfortable?

Comfort depends on weight, clamping pressure, headband design and earcup cushioning. Lighter headphones aren’t automatically more comfortable: how the headband distributes weight matters, too.

Look for enough adjustment to position the earcups comfortably around your ears, with a secure fit that doesn’t squeeze. Glasses can affect both comfort and the seal. Cushion materials also matter, particularly if heat and sweating become uncomfortable during longer sessions.

Try headphones for an extended session if possible, checking for pressure around your ears and across your head. For travel, consider whether they fold and whether the supplied case provides adequate protection.

How much battery life do I need?

Choose enough battery life for your longest listening sessions, with some allowance for missed charges. Around 30 hours with ANC enabled is a useful target for commuting and occasional travel, while frequent travelers may prefer longer endurance. A shorter runtime can still be sufficient if you recharge regularly.

Compare figures under the same conditions: turning off ANC can substantially increase battery life. Our reviews distinguish manufacturers’ estimates from measured results where available.

Quick charging can be as useful as total endurance, providing enough playback for a journey after a short charge. For longer trips, check whether headphones work while charging or through a cable with an empty battery. Wired listening doesn’t necessarily mean battery-free listening.

What is Auracast?

Auracast lets a compatible source broadcast audio to multiple headphones or hearing devices. It can be useful for shared listening or receiving audio in equipped public venues. Check explicitly for Auracast reception support; a recent Bluetooth version alone doesn’t guarantee it.

Buying advice: What to look for when buying headphones

Below, we run through what to look for when choosing over-ear headphones for your iPhone or Mac, from sound quality and comfort to Apple features, lossless audio, noise cancellation and battery life.

Which headphone features matter for iPhone and Mac users?

Sound quality, comfort and reliable connectivity should come first. AAC support is useful for Bluetooth listening on Apple devices, but it isn’t required for basic compatibility. Check which additional features work with your iPhone, iPad and Mac, including easy pairing, automatic switching, hands-free Siri and Find My. These vary between models – even within Apple’s AirPods and Beats ranges.

Bluetooth multipoint lets compatible headphones maintain connections to two devices, making it useful for moving between an iPhone and Mac. Check how switching works in practice, rather than assuming it behaves like Apple’s automatic switching. Also check whether the manufacturer’s iPhone app offers equalizer controls and firmware updates.

Prioritize listening assessments over driver size or frequency-response claims. Look for clear vocals, audible detail and bass that suits your taste without overwhelming the music.

Can I listen to Apple Music lossless through headphones?

Yes, but the connection matters. Standard Bluetooth playback from an iPhone or Mac uses compression, even when you select a lossless track in Apple Music. A compatible wired connection is the straightforward way to hear lossless audio.

AirPods Max 2 and the first-generation USB-C AirPods Max support lossless playback over USB-C with current software and firmware. Some competing wireless headphones, including Beats Studio Pro, also offer USB audio. However, a USB-C charging port doesn’t necessarily support audio, so check before buying.

Traditional headphones with a 3.5mm plug are another option. Depending on your device, you may need an adapter or an external digital-to-analog converter (DAC). The supported resolution depends on the entire connection; wired listening doesn’t automatically guarantee support for Apple Music’s highest-resolution recordings. See our guide to DACs and lossless audio on iPhone and Mac.

Some headphones include a wireless transmitter. Check its compatibility and supported formats: adding a transmitter doesn’t automatically make playback lossless.

How much noise cancellation do I need?

For frequent flights, train journeys or noisy workplaces, prioritize effective active noise cancellation (ANC). It is particularly useful against steady sounds such as engine drone. Performance against conversations and sudden noises varies, so look for listening-test results rather than relying on manufacturers’ claims.

Passive isolation comes from the earcups sealing around your ears. A good fit helps both isolation and sound quality. Transparency or ambient modes use microphones to let you hear your surroundings without removing the headphones – useful when listening for announcements or maintaining awareness while walking.

If you make frequent calls, assess microphone performance separately: effective listening ANC doesn’t guarantee clear speech for the person you’re calling.

What makes over-ear headphones comfortable?

Comfort depends on weight, clamping pressure, headband design and earcup cushioning. Lighter headphones aren’t automatically more comfortable: how the headband distributes weight matters, too.

Look for enough adjustment to position the earcups comfortably around your ears, with a secure fit that doesn’t squeeze. Glasses can affect both comfort and the seal. Cushion materials also matter, particularly if heat and sweating become uncomfortable during longer sessions.

Try headphones for an extended session if possible, checking for pressure around your ears and across your head. For travel, consider whether they fold and whether the supplied case provides adequate protection.

How much battery life do I need?

Choose enough battery life for your longest listening sessions, with some allowance for missed charges. Around 30 hours with ANC enabled is a useful target for commuting and occasional travel, while frequent travelers may prefer longer endurance. A shorter runtime can still be sufficient if you recharge regularly.

Compare figures under the same conditions: turning off ANC can substantially increase battery life. Our reviews distinguish manufacturers’ estimates from measured results where available.

Quick charging can be as useful as total endurance, providing enough playback for a journey after a short charge. For longer trips, check whether headphones work while charging or through a cable with an empty battery. Wired listening doesn’t necessarily mean battery-free listening.

What is Auracast?

Auracast lets a compatible source broadcast audio to multiple headphones or hearing devices. It can be useful for shared listening or receiving audio in equipped public venues. Check explicitly for Auracast reception support; a recent Bluetooth version alone doesn’t guarantee it.

How Macworld reviews headphones

When our audio experts review headphones our comprehensive evaluation covers sound quality, design and comfort, key features like noise cancellation, and overall value for money. We undertake subjective listening tests and an objective analysis of features and build quality.

The most critical aspect of our headphone reviews is an assessment of audio performance including Tonal Balance, Clarity and Detail, Audio Defects and Spatial Audio.

Active Noise Cancellation and Transparency Modes are also assessed, both being primary features users look for. We test how effectively the headphones block out different types of ambient sound, such as the low-frequency drone of an airplane engine versus higher-frequency chatter. We also assess how well transparency mode amplify outside sounds when you need to be aware of your surroundings.

Design, comfort and build quality are also important factors, as is the ease of use when it comes to the controls and functionality. Battery life is another important consideration, and the time it takes to charge the headphones.

Finally, we review the available connection options and the codecs supported since AAC support is required for Apple devices.

According to a research project by Derik Kauffman, Apple has a built-in list of words and phrases that the keyboard suggested words will never complete, and the swiping keyboard will not produce. This isn’t a censorship list—typing individual characters always works—but it can slow you down if you’re looking to use swiping or suggested words to speed up your iPhone typing.

The project is detailed at Swipeblocked.com, with additional code and data hosted on GitHub. There, Kauffman details his forensics to discover this feature and the blocked phrases.

Here’s how it works: Apple has built into iOS a hash table of “blocked” phrases. It’s not storing plain text of words, but rather matching hashes of word IDs to a set of banned hashes. If there’s a match, the iOS keyboard will not suggest the word. And if you are swiping, it will either input some other word for your swiped word or replace an earlier word in your phrase with a different word that has a similar swipe pattern.

The list of phrases has not been made public by Apple, and the company does not disclose how it chooses what goes on it. Kauffman reverse-engineered it from the hash table within iOS.

The phrases are mostly what you would expect. They include vulgarities, politically and socially charged phrases, rascist terms, various forms of bigotry, and so on. You can literally type out the phrase, “smoking weed,” but if you type “smoking wee…” then the keyboard suggestions to finish off that second word will never include the obvious “weed.” Instead, you’ll get “weekend” or “weekly.” And if you’re using Apple’s QuickPath (Slide to Type), you’ll get “smoking Wed” or some other word, no matter how precise you are about swiping the word “weed” correctly.

The Swipeblocked site has a list of all the English-language banned phrases in iOS 27. Warning: Many of them are not safe for work and highly offensive. But some are things that you may very well wish to type or swipe, especially in a particular context (illegal immigrant, NBA surveillance, etc.), and the refusal of the iOS keyboard to complete swiping entry or suggest the natural next word is one reason users are frustrated with it.

In addition to the phrases that are blocked from the suggested word area or swiping, there is a mechanism to prevent the autocomplete and suggested word list from suggesting individual words. The iOS dictionary labels words as either vulgar, offensive, or sensitive. Vulgar words are not suggested until the user manually types them three times. Offensive words are never suggested or completed by swiping (though you can always type them out yourself). Sensitive words are similarly never offered as a prediction or completion, and some of them can’t be swiped.

Why does Apple do all this? It’s likely less about policing your speech than it is about avoiding lawsuits and bad PR. All it takes is one person posting a screenshot of the iOS keyboard suggesting the word “good” after they type “The Nazis were” or “real” after Santa isn’t” (both included in the list) to cause a bad viral moment criticizing Apple’s intentions, even if the keyboard suggestions would only suggest things that the user had typed several times before.

However, it’s still overreaching. A good solution would be to give users a choice. Allow a keyboard setting, enabled by default, to moderate the suggested word list and swipe keyboard to avoid offensive content, but also give users the ability to turn it off. But until then, you’ll need to type a little more slowly if you want to write certain phrases.

How to watch A Charlie Brown Thanksgiving for free on Apple TV

On November 15 and 16, anyone with an Apple ID can watch A Charlie Brown Thanksgiving. If you own an Apple device, you have one, but if not, Apple IDs are free and you don’t need a credit card to sign up. Once you have signed up, you can watch in several ways:

  • Through the TV app on an iPhone, iPad, or Mac.
  • On smart TVs with the Apple TV app.
  • On the web at tv.apple.com.
  • On an Apple TV device.

Gaming subscription services are all the rage now, but Apple Arcade isn’t a little different from the likes of PlayStation Plus, EA Play, or Xbox Game Pass. If you’ve got questions about it, we’ve got plenty of answers.

Updated November 6, 2026: There are four new games on the service this month: Crossy Road Rush, Food Stylist — Design Game+, KAMI 2+, NBA 2K7 Arcade Edition.

What is Apple Arcade?

Apple Arcade is a gaming subscription service for iPhone, iPad, Mac, and AppleTV that features several hundred games. The games are a mix of genres and styles, and include original games you’ll only find on the service and others that can be found on the regular App Store or even other platforms. Apple Arcade isn’t a streaming service like Xbox Live Cloud Gaming or GeForce NOW. Games must be downloaded onto your device in order to be played.

What do I need to run it?

Apple Arcade was made available as part of iOS 13, iPad OS 13, tvOS 13, and macOS Catalina or later. Some of the more visually-intensive games may only run well on newer hardware, though, and some Mac games require macOS 11 (Big Sur).

How much does Apple Arcade cost?

Apple Arcade costs $6.99/£6.99 per month, and you’ll also get a one-month free trial or you can get three months free if you purchase a new iPhone, iPad, Apple TV or Mac. To claim your free trial click here.

You can get Apple Arcade for less than $6.99 a month if you subscribe for a year upfront. A year of Apple Arcade is $49.99/£49.99 (so $4.16 a month). If you’re currently on the $6.99 month-to-month plan and want to switch to the annual plan and save some money, you can do so on your iPhone or iPad. Open the App Store app, then tap your account icon in the upper right. Tap Subscriptions, then tap the entry for Apple Arcade. Here, you can switch to the annual plan.

Apple Arcade is also included in the Apple One subscription bundles, which range from $20 a month to $38 a month and include access to Apple Music and Apple TV and iCloud storage. There is also a month free trial of Apple One. To claim the trial, or sign up for Apple One, click here.

How do I sign up for Apple Arcade?

There isn’t an Apple Arcade app—it’s built into the App Store. On your iPhone, iPad, or Mac open the App Store and look for the Apple Arcade tab at the bottom of the screen (or in the left column on macOS). A sign-up screen with a Try It Free button will appear. After the trial you’ll be charged either the monthly or annual fee, depending on your selection. When subscribing, you’ll need to enter your Apple ID password or use Touch ID or Face ID to sign in, and you’ll have to confirm your subscription purchase a few times.

Once you’re done with the sign up, the Arcade section of the App Store shows what games are available to you. To access a game, tap on it in the App Store, then tap the Get button. When the game is done installing on your device, the Get button turns into a Play button, and you can tap it to launch the game. The game app icon will also appear on your device’s Home page.

On the Apple TV, there actually is an Arcade app. Open that to see the sign-up offer. You’ll also find an Arcade tab within the App Store.

Does my subscription include family sharing?

Yes. One $6.99 per month subscription can be shared between up to six people (including you).

How do I cancel Apple Arcade?

First off, keep in mind that if you cancel Apple Arcade (either before your free trial is up or after subscribing), you won’t be able to keep playing the games unless you re-subscribe. If you’re okay with that, you can use the same process you use to cancel any other subscription service. Here’s the easiest way to do it on the iPhone and iPad:

  1. Open the App Store app and tap on your profile photo in the upper right.
  2. In the screen that pops up, press Subscriptions near the top of the page.
  3. You’ll then see a list of active subscriptions, and Apple Arcade should be listed there. Tap it.
  4. You’ll either see Cancel Free Trial or Cancel Subscription toward the middle of the page that appears. Tap whatever option is available, then Confirm Cancellation.

And here’s how to cancel Apple Arcade on the Mac:

  1. Open the App Store app and then press the icon with your profile photo in the lower left.
  2. The Account window will appear, and you should then click View Information at the top of the window. Enter your password when/if prompted.
  3. When your Account Information appears, scroll down to the Manage section and click the Manage link to the right of Subscriptions.
  4. When the list of your active subscriptions appears, click Edit to the right of Apple Arcade.
  5. Toward the middle of the page that appears, you’ll see a button that says either Cancel Free Trial or Cancel Subscription. Click it, then click Confirm Cancellation and Confirm.

Do Apple Arcade games have in-app purchases?

No. In Apple’s words, “since every game includes access to the full experience, including all game features, content, and future updates, no additional purchases will be required.” Even games that have in-app purchases on the App Store won’t have any in Apple Arcade.

Do Apple Arcade games have ads?

Also no. On a related note, Apple says Apple Arcade has no ad tracking.

Is Apple Arcade a game streaming service like GeForce NOW or Xbox Game Streaming?

No. All Apple Arcade games are downloaded.

Are there demos for Apple Arcade games?

No, and they’re not really necessary. Like regular App Store apps, games download quickly and can easily be removed if you don’t want to keep it anymore.

Apple partly envisions Apple Arcade as a way of letting players try out games with more freedom than the App Store currently allows (which is basically none). In Apple’s words, “rather than pay upfront for each game, a subscription to Apple Arcade will give players the opportunity to try any game in the service without risk.”

The service has a free trial, though, as we’ve seen with other Apple subscription services.

Am I able to keep playing Apple Arcade games if I cancel my subscription?

No. As with most subscription services, you only have access while you’re a subscriber.

Can I use controllers with Apple Arcade games?

Yes. In additional to traditional MFi (Made for iOS) controllers, you can pair some specific Bluetooth controllers for either PlayStation or Xbox with your iPhone, iPad, or Apple TV. Since many Apple Arcade games are playable on Mac and Apple TV (where controller support is more common), many games will support them. Some games, especially those that are also available in the broader App Store and only for iPhone or iPad, have no controller support.

How often are new games released?

Games are typically released on the first Friday of each month. There are some rare exceptions.

What games have been released so far?

There are over 200 games available for Apple Arcade, and the list grows all the time.

Live Rewind, one of the more compelling features demonstrated at the launch of the Apple Watch Series 12 back in September, has finally become available with the launch (in beta form) of watchOS 27.3 and iOS 27.3. I’ve spent several days testing Live Rewind, and can report that it’s a thoroughly impressive proof of concept. But there are flaws and limitations to be aware of, even if several of the latter are the result of good intentions.

Here are six takeaways from my extensive hands-on testing with Live Rewind on the Apple Watch Series 12.

Live Rewind is surprisingly accurate

I was skeptical, but Live Rewind does a surprisingly decent job of understanding and transcribing what it hears.

I started by playing YouTube videos of restaurant conversations for people learning English as a foreign language: slow, clear, with largely simple vocabulary. I sat close to the iPad playing the video. An easy task to begin with, and Live Rewind coped easily. The transcripts were virtually perfect, not to mention beautifully formatted with line breaks to denote separate short speeches.

I stepped up the difficulty by looking up some menus online (I selected this fancy restaurant) and acting the part of the waiter myself. I selected esoteric dishes I hadn’t heard of, spoke quickly and was careless with my enunciation, chucked in some ums and ers, varied volume and occasionally mumbled a little. And the feature produced a mostly accurate transcript that would have been extremely useful to a diner who had missed an option on the list.

This time the formatting was more of a challenge–Live Rewind couldn’t keep track of separate sentences, so the whole thing was jumbled together with a sometimes misleading number of commas–and occasionally I had to decipher a soundalike guess when the feature didn’t recognise a term. (“IV” instead of Ivy, “7 and Y” instead of the British rivers Severn and Wye, for example.) But the information was mostly there.

The most difficult task was when I used Live Rewind (after obtaining consent!) to recall snatches of random conversations with my family. This was more mixed. It caught the gist a lot of the time. But there were more soundalike guesses than before, and some sentences were missed entirely. This mostly related to distance, I think, and I’ll come back to that later.

So Live Recall is by no means perfect. But considering the difficulty of the task–handling variations in accent and diction, mumbling and muffled speech, irregular grammar, slang, in-jokes, proper nouns, brand names, technical or foreign terms–it does a very solid job. My verdict is that the accuracy is high enough to be useful as backup if you missed something, but not yet accurate enough to depend on as an alternative to paying attention.

David Price / Foundry

Live Rewind has a short memory

Like the proverbial goldfish, Live Rewind has a memory of 15 seconds. Which is shorter than you might think.

On one test I read out a list of just four main courses, but made sure to include the additional verbiage for each one, as I suspect many waiters in high-end establishments would be encouraged to do. Nothing extreme, just an extra sentence detailing ingredients and/or preparation. The result of this slight bulking out was that Live Rewind, despite being triggered the very moment I finished my list, missed a big chunk of it. The first main and half the second were lost to history.

Bear in mind, too, that while lists of specials in restaurants may frequently fit in the 15-second window (assuming the waiter refrains from prolixity), other scenarios may not work so well. Will the list of cocktails at a bar fit in 15 seconds, or the list of films at a cinema, or the list of changes your boss told you to make to a document? I have my doubts, although Siri Recap, if you use it, does not have a time limit and may be able to step in.

The short memory, it’s worth noting, applies whether or not Live Rewind is currently hearing anything. If you trigger the feature, it won’t rewind to the last 15 seconds of audio it heard; it will show you any speech it has heard in the past 15 seconds, ending when you double-press the Digital Crown. If you’ve been sitting in silence for at least 15 seconds, you’ll see the message “No voice detected.”

And even if you do manage to capture the transcript of some speech, Live Rewind will by default forget it the moment you tap the X button to close it. You need to explicitly save it to the Siri app if you want to keep the record. (You’ll save only the transcript, needless to say, not the audio from which it was created.)

This short memory is deliberate, by the way, as we’ll discover.

Live Rewind has a short range

My first impressions of the feature were not good. When I tried to use it on a conversation with my daughter, who was sitting perhaps 6 or 8 meters away and speaking unusually clearly, it produced a transcript of all my words and literally none of hers. But after more testing it became apparent that this was an issue of range, not accuracy. Live Rewind is good at picking up speech that’s close to you, and far less effective when someone is speaking even from the other side of the room.

I haven’t been able to find any evidence that this is deliberate (I know, for example, that the closely related feature Siri Recap can and will listen to people further away, since Apple gives the example of a lecturer “in an otherwise quiet room” in its notes) but suspect that it may relate to privacy. If the waiter leans in and tells you about today’s delicious cod cheeks, one may assume they consent to being heard. If the speaker is three tables away, things become murkier.

Live Rewind doesn’t approve of swearing

I don’t want to shock you, but while testing this feature I happened to hear a YouTuber use the word “shit.” Live Rewind transcribed this as ****. (Siri Recap did the same, incidentally.)

The closest I can find to an explanation is in the support document, where Apple says Siri Recap is “designed to omit potentially harmful content, such as language that promotes self-harm or hateful speech.” But that’s a different issue, and “shit” does not, as far as I can see, constitute hateful speech.

So it’s a bit of a mystery. But very much the sort of family-values prudishness we’ve come to expect from Apple.

David Price / Foundry

The range of privacy measures is admirable…

For better and worse, the issue of privacy is absolutely central to Live Rewind.

Apple is conscious that most of us are creeped out by the idea of a wrist-mounted surveillance bot listening in on conversations. It’s conscious that previous surveillance-adjacent tech (Google Glass, for example) has encountered significant public pushback, and wants to avoid bad PR. So everything has been done with privacy in mind.

To trigger Live Rewind, you have to double-press the Digital Crown, a distinctive gesture intended to be hard for creeps to disguise. A similar intent lies behind the on-screen animation and non-mutable sound effect, both of which alert anyone close enough to be recorded by the feature that you are summoning a transcript of what they just said.

It’s also worth mentioning that the feature works on your device. (The processing legwork happens on the companion iPhone, not the Apple Watch, by the way, so make sure it’s nearby.) It doesn’t happen in the cloud, and Apple insists it does not have access to the data.

I won’t pretend I’m completely on board with listening tech in general. I fear that such technologies are becoming more and more widespread and normalised. But with Live Rewind, Apple has done everything it can to take privacy concerns into consideration.

…and sometimes frustrating

I applaud Apple for its efforts to safeguard privacy. But like the AirTag, which quite rightly took steps to combat stalking and in the process made itself a far less effective anti-theft device, Live Rewind finds itself in a position where good intentions lead to many of its most frustrating limitations.

The short memory is there to limit the feature’s surveillance capabilities. Ditto, I suspect, the short physical range. It also doesn’t attempt, by design and for explicitly privacy-related reasons, to identify or differentiate between multiple speakers (not even “speaker A” and “speaker B”), despite this being an obvious way to make transcripts easier to parse.

When viewing the transcript on your Apple Watch, you’ll find that the screenshot function is disabled, presumably to make it slightly less convenient for bad actors to eavesdrop and then share the results. But this also makes life less convenient if you want to share them for innocent reasons, such as sending the list of specials to a latecomer on their way to the restaurant, or publishing an article about how well the feature works.

Live Rewind would be much more useful if these limitations were cast aside, but it would also be more controversial, and Apple doesn’t like that.

Mahmoud Itani / Foundry

Conclusions

I’m way more impressed by Live Rewind than I expected to be.

The accuracy is very solid. Yes, it makes some mistakes when tested under the most challenging conditions, but a lot of those mistakes will actually be phonetic best guesses that can be deciphered with little effort. And it usually gets the important details right.

It’s not quite sharp enough that you can ignore the waiter listing off specials or the senior colleague asking you a question and assume everything will be transcribed perfectly. But it’s a handy backup for the parts you missed while mostly paying attention.

The main issues I have with Live Rewind, if they can be called issues, are the limitations deliberately put in place for privacy reasons. It’s got very short range, for instance, and the 15-second memory window is on the low side in terms of usefulness. But privacy matters, and I understand why Apple made these decisions.

Speaking only for myself, I still find the concept a tiny bit creepy. But Apple has done its best to minimise that factor, and this is overall a very decent effort.

With the MacBook Pro with PROLED Display, Apple returned the Apple logo to its former glory, switching from shiny aluminum to one that lights up and glows again. And it’s got a new trick: Turn up the display brightness, and the logo gets brighter, too. Turn down the display brightness, and the logo dims.

However, since the brightness controls on the display and logo are linked, the only way to turn the brightness on the logo all the way down is to also turn off the display. And sadly, Apple did not include a system setting control for the logo, so you can’t turn it off by simply flicking a switch.

But you can turn it off through Terminal, Apple’s command line interface for the Mac. In fact, Apple has a support document with the details.

Turn off the glowing Apple logo

  1. You must be logged into the Mac with an account that has Administrator rights.
  2. Launch Terminal. It is in Applications>Utilities. You can also press Command + Space to bring up Spotlight Search, type “Terminal,” and press Return after “Terminal — Open” appears in the search box.
  3. Copy the following and paste it into Terminal sudo defaults write com.apple.CoreBrightness LEBacklightMode -int 0 then press Return
  4. Terminal will ask for your password, which must be a user with Administrator rights. (When typing the password, Terminal will not show the characters.) Press Return and the logo should turn off.
  5. Quit Terminal.

Turn on the glowing Apple logo

Follow the same steps as above, but enter this Terminal command: sudo defaults delete com.apple.CoreBrightness LEBacklightMode

The glowing Apple logo is on by default, so if you reinstall macOS after turning it off, it will turn back on.
